title: John Abraham Studied Rakesh Maria's Mind, Not His Mannerisms. The 26/11 Biopic Is Nearly Ready.
excerpt: Rohit Shetty trades his fictional cop universe for the real thing — and John Abraham's portrayal of India's most decorated police commissioner might be his most intense role yet
body:
Key Takeaways
  • John Abraham portrays Rakesh Maria, a pivotal figure in Mumbai's police history.
  • The film *Maria IPS* is based on Maria's memoir detailing his career.
  • Rohit Shetty shifts from fictional to real-life storytelling in this project.
  • The production involved shooting at 40 real locations in Mumbai.
  • The film aims to resonate with the Indian diaspora affected by the 26/11 attacks.
There is a moment in every actor's career when the role stops being a character and starts becoming a responsibility. For **John Abraham**, that moment arrived the day he agreed to play **Rakesh Maria** — the former Commissioner of Mumbai Police whose career reads less like a résumé and more like a thriller franchise that nobody needed to fictionalise. The film, directed by **Rohit Shetty** and likely titled *Maria IPS*, is based on Maria's 2020 memoir *Let Me Say It Now*. It marks the first time Shetty — the architect of Bollywood's most commercially successful cop universe, from *Singham* to *Sooryavanshi* — has stepped away from fictional heroics to tell a story rooted entirely in real events. And what events they are. Maria's career intersected with nearly every defining moment of Mumbai's modern history. As Deputy Commissioner of Police in 1993, he cracked the Bombay serial blasts case that killed 257 people and shook the nation's conscience. A decade later, he solved the 2003 Gateway of India and Zaveri Bazaar twin blasts, arresting six suspects including a couple who had planted explosives inside taxis. And in 2008, he was handed the investigation that would define his legacy: the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks. Maria personally interrogated **Ajmal Kasab**, the sole surviving gunman, in sessions that helped unravel the full scope of the Pakistani-coordinated assault that left 166 dead. This is not a man whose life can be captured through a uniform and a salute. In a candid interview published this weekend, Abraham made clear he understands the weight of what he's carrying. > "Rakesh Maria is someone whose career has intersected with some defining moments in our country's history, so naturally there's a tremendous sense of responsibility in portraying him." — John Abraham What's striking about Abraham's approach is his refusal to treat the role as impersonation. "When you are portraying a real person, the objective isn't imitation — it's understanding the individual behind the public image," he said. "That means spending a lot of time researching, understanding his mindset, the pressures he faced, and the decisions he had to make." Shetty, for his part, has matched that seriousness with the production itself. The film was shot across forty real locations in South and Central Mumbai — the same streets Maria patrolled, the same neighbourhoods where bombs went off and gunmen opened fire. A full-scale police station set was constructed at Ellora Studios in Mira Road for the interrogation sequences, built for authenticity rather than spectacle. At its peak, the shoot involved fifty to a hundred crew members on set daily. **Tamannaah Bhatia** plays **Preeti Maria**, the officer's wife — a woman who, as one source put it, "supported him through some of the most dangerous and testing moments of his career." It is Tamannaah's second collaboration with Abraham after *Vedaa*, and her first project under Shetty's direction. The production reportedly wrapped its principal photography in a concentrated 45-day schedule between March and June. Shetty, known for his meticulous planning and relentless pace, wanted an uninterrupted shoot — no breaks, no parallel commitments.

First Collaboration with Rohit Shetty
For the Indian diaspora, this is a film that hits differently. The 26/11 attacks didn't just happen to Mumbai — they happened to every Indian who watched the Taj burn on live television from apartments in New Jersey, living rooms in London, offices in Dubai. Maria's memoir, which sold widely in overseas Indian communities, gave readers the view from inside the investigation that most news coverage never could. A theatrical adaptation of that perspective, backed by Shetty's commercial instincts and Abraham's physical commitment, has the ingredients of something genuinely powerful. Shetty himself put it plainly: "Rakesh Maria, the man who stared terror in the face for 36 years. His incredible journey spans all the way from the 1993 blasts in Mumbai, the underworld menace, to the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks in 2008. Feel truly honoured to be bringing this real-life super cop's brave and fearless journey to the screen." Maria responded in kind: "It is exciting to re-live the journey, especially when piloted by a brilliant director like Rohit Shetty. More than the nostalgia, it's also a valuable opportunity to place before the people the extraordinary work of the Mumbai Police." Abraham also spoke about how his taste in projects has shifted. "I think every story should leave you with something," he said. "Entertainment is important — cinema should always engage you — but if a film also stays with you after you've left the theatre, that's even better. I'm not choosing projects because they're trying to make a statement; I'm choosing them because I believe they're honest, well told and emotionally engaging." For a man who built his career on six-pack abs and stylised action, this feels like a genuine pivot. And for Rohit Shetty — who has spent two decades making fictional cops look invincible — telling the story of a real one who simply did his job under impossible pressure might be the most ambitious thing he's ever attempted. A release date has not been officially announced. But the film is finished, the edit is underway, and by all accounts, *Maria IPS* is coming sooner than anyone expected.
